name: Lena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We run Hartwell Farm, a hundred and ten hectares, with a few of everything: forty beef cattle, a flock of two hundred ewes, some barley, a field of potatoes and a big vegetable garden. The heart of it is the farm shop in the old cart shed. Most mornings I check stock first, then I'm in the shop by nine, cutting cheese and talking to people, and the afternoons are whatever the farm needs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Joao does the butchery, he trained as a butcher in his twenties before we met. Then there's Marjorie on the till, who's sixty-four and knows everyone's business, and two part-timers, Precious and a student called Finn. So five of us, plus my brother when it's lambing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people can see where their food comes from. A child stands at the fence and watches the lambs and then goes in and buys lamb chops, and I think that's honest. What wears me out is the pricing, trying to keep the shop affordable for the village and still pay four people properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Finn set me up with one to write the shop newsletter and the signs, because I'd spend a whole evening on a paragraph. It writes too politely, so I always rough it up a bit. I don't let it near the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, carry on. If it helps me write the newsletter faster and does nothing else, that's a nice small thing. At the farmers' market I'd say the real issues are still feed prices and the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing changes, and that's a relief. The shop does well because people trust us, and a better search engine doesn't change trust. I'd still be fretting about Marjorie's hip and whether she'll retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the plan we already had. That's a new cold room for Joao's butchery, about eleven thousand, and maybe a stall at the Saturday market in town. I'd use the AI tool a bit more for the website, if Finn showed me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. It's a normal year, and normal years are good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Marjorie retiring. What would that mean for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be a hole. She knows that Mr Hughes is diabetic and steers him off the fudge, and that the Kowalskis are short this month so she rounds down. You can't hire that. You can only grow it, over twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the shop where a tool like that would actually help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, maybe. I always over-order cheese at Christmas and end up eating it in January. If something told me I sold forty wedges of the blue last year, not sixty, that would save me a few hundred pounds and some weight.

S0.say: I'd say fine, carry on, if it helps write the newsletter faster. The real issues at the market are still feed prices and the bank.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief that nothing changes. The shop works because people trust us, and a better search engine doesn't touch that.
S0.do: Goes ahead with the planned eleven-thousand cold room for Joao's butchery and looks at a Saturday market stall. Uses the AI tool a little more for the website and Christmas cheese ordering.
S0.feel: Calm and content, a normal good year.
S0.quote: You can't hire that. You can only grow it, over twenty years.
S0.fieldNote: She defines the value of the shop through Marjorie's knowledge of customers, not the produce. Light, warm and practical. Her one wish for AI is modest and specific: stop her over-ordering cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to protect young people's first jobs, through apprenticeships, public money, whatever it takes. I'd write that in the newsletter, actually, because half our customers have kids looking for work. I might get some angry emails, but I'd stand by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means I've got time. The farm and the shop will look much the same in ten years. But Finn is doing an accounts degree, and the first jobs he'd apply for are exactly the ones they'd stop hiring for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer Finn more hours, and maybe a proper role doing the shop's books and website, so he has something real on his CV. That's maybe two thousand more a year in wages, which we can just about carry. I'd also talk to the agricultural college about taking a placement student at lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the way you feel when it's a dry spring. Nothing's wrong yet, but you're watching the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire Finn to do the books. You said you don't let the AI near the accounts. Why trust him and not it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can look Finn in the eye. If the VAT is wrong, I can ask him why, and he goes red and fixes it. With the tool I don't know who to ask. Maybe that's old-fashioned, but it's my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write in that newsletter, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, the lamb's in, the leeks are good, and by the way, if you know a young person looking for a start, send them to us. We can't take many, but we'll take one. I'd keep it short. People read it for the recipes.

S1.say: I'd say we have to protect young people's first jobs with apprenticeships and public money. I'd write it in the shop newsletter and stand by it even if I got angry emails.
S1.think: Privately I think slow gives me time and the farm will look the same in ten years. My worry is Finn, whose accounts degree points at exactly the beginner jobs that would vanish.
S1.do: Offers Finn more hours and a proper role doing the shop's books and website, about two thousand a year more in wages. Contacts the agricultural college about a lambing placement student.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a dry spring when you keep watching the sky.
S1.quote: Because I can look Finn in the eye. If the VAT is wrong, I can ask him why, and he goes red and fixes it.
S1.fieldNote: Steady in the true sense: she would act, but carefully and within what she can afford. Her trust in people over tools is about being able to hold someone to account. The newsletter shows how she mixes politics with recipes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, with retraining and support, before people lose their homes. I'd say it at the shop counter, gently, and more loudly on the local farmers' group. I think politicians arguing loudly and doing nothing is the worst of both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honest bit is that my customers are office people. Our best spenders on a Saturday are commuters, the ones who work at the bank and the council. If they lose their jobs or their pay drops, they'll go back to the supermarket, and the shop's takings could fall by a quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a cheaper range straight away, mince, stewing lamb, soup bags, the kind of thing a family on a tight budget can still buy from us. I'd hold off on the market stall and the cold room for a year, and keep that eleven thousand in the bank. And I'd talk to the staff honestly about hours, before I'd cut anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've seen bad years, but properly anxious about the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to the staff about hours. Who'd be hardest to talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious. She's a single mum with two boys, and those twenty hours a week are her rent. I'd cut my own hours in the shop before hers, and Joao's. We can eat the leftover sausages. She can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did you think the farm shop would be hit by an office-job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not until you asked. I'd always thought of us as safe from that sort of thing, because you can't email a lamb. But we sell to people, and people's wages are where the money comes from. That's a bit of a cold shower, actually.

S2.say: I'd say the government must step in now with retraining and support before people lose their homes. Politicians arguing loudly and doing nothing is the worst of both.
S2.think: Privately I realise my best Saturday customers are office workers from the bank and the council. If their pay drops they'll go back to the supermarket and the shop's takings could fall by a quarter.
S2.do: Launches a cheaper range of mince, stewing lamb and soup bags straight away. Postpones the eleven-thousand cold room and market stall for a year, and cuts her own and Joao's hours before touching staff.
S2.feel: Anxious about the shop, though not panicked, because she's lived through bad years.
S2.quote: I'd cut my own hours in the shop before hers, and Joao's. We can eat the leftover sausages. She can't.
S2.fieldNote: She discovered her own exposure mid-interview: the shop depends on office wages. That realisation visibly shifted her mood. Her first instinct is to protect the lowest-paid worker, which matches her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tax the gains, absolutely, and use them for the people who lost their jobs. I'd be at the meetings, I'd sign the letters. I'd also say the countryside will fill up with rich people buying second homes, and somebody has to make sure the village survives that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a strange mix for us. The village will fill with people who've made fortunes on shares and houses, and they'll love a posh farm shop, so takings might actually go up. But the people who've lost their jobs won't be shopping with us at all, and Precious and Marjorie's families might be among them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be careful not to turn the shop into a place only rich people can afford. I'd keep the cheaper range and put a pay-what-you-can shelf by the door, for bread and veg. With the extra takings from the newcomers, I'd raise Precious and Finn's pay a bit. And I'd finally build Joao's cold room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit guilty. We might do well out of something that's hurting a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise your prices for the newcomers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On some things, yes, the fancy cheese and the dry-aged beef. Joao would say charge what the market pays. But not on the basics. I'm not putting the price of a loaf up because a man from the city has a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel guilty. Who'd you feel it in front of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marjorie, I think. Her son-in-law is an architect, and if those jobs go, I'd see it on her face at the till every morning. Doing well while your friends struggle is not as nice as people imagine.

S3.say: I'd say tax the gains and use them for people who lost their jobs. Somebody also has to make sure the village survives a wave of rich second-home buyers.
S3.think: Privately I think the shop might actually do better with rich newcomers buying posh food. But the people who lost their jobs would stop shopping, and Marjorie's and Precious's families might be among them.
S3.do: Keeps the cheaper range, adds a pay-what-you-can shelf for bread and veg, and raises Precious's and Finn's pay from the newcomers' spending. Finally builds Joao's cold room.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a little guilty about doing well while others suffer.
S3.quote: I'm not putting the price of a loaf up because a man from the city has a new car.
S3.fieldNote: Her mood is lower here than in the previous picture, because the shop might profit. The guilt is real and tied to faces she sees daily. She splits prices into luxuries and basics, which is her politics turned into shop policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people must come first, and robots on farms need rules, who owns them, who gets the money. I'd want the farmers' union and the farm workers' union in the same room for once. And I'd say loudly that a farm shop is about people, and I'm keeping it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the farm side scares me. If big farms have robots picking veg and handling sheep, their prices drop, and the supermarket gets cheaper again. We'd survive on trust and the shop, but the gap between our price and theirs would get very wide. And people with no jobs don't pay for trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see if the robots actually work in mud and on our slopes before buying anything. I'd lean harder into what a robot can't do: farm walks, lambing days for schools, Joao's butchery classes. I'd talk to the bank about our overdraft, which is about twenty thousand, in case the first year is bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the one where I can't see what the shop looks like in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. What would you need to see before you'd buy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see one on a farm like ours, not a demo on a flat field. If Gwen at Pen-y-Bryn has one and it can sort ewes in the rain without hurting them, I'd go and have a cup of tea with her and watch. Then I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the school kids on those farm walks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth. That a person who knows animals can tell a ewe is in trouble by the way she stands, and maybe a robot can learn that too, but somebody should still be watching. And then I'd let them hold a lamb, because that's why they come.

S4.say: I'd say people must come first and farm robots need rules about who owns them and who gets the money. A farm shop is about people, and I'm keeping it that way.
S4.think: Privately the farm side scares me, because big farms with robots would make supermarket food even cheaper. We'd survive on trust, but people with no jobs don't pay for trust.
S4.do: Waits a year to see robots work on a farm like hers before buying. Expands farm walks, school lambing days and Joao's butchery classes, and talks to the bank about the twenty-thousand overdraft.
S4.feel: Alarmed, because she can't picture the shop five years on.
S4.quote: We'd survive on trust and the shop, but the gap between our price and theirs would get very wide. And people with no jobs don't pay for trust.
S4.fieldNote: She stays practical even when alarmed, with a clear test for buying a robot: seeing one work at a neighbour's farm. Her plan leans on selling the human experience. She knows that plan depends on customers still having wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, I think, because it hits both ends, the farm costs and the customers. What would help is the government actually sharing the gains, so people still have wages to spend in places like ours. And some help for small farms to buy robots together, as a cooperative, so it's not only the big boys who get them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the village. A farm shop is one of the last places people bump into each other. If it closes, it's not just my job, it's Mr Hughes not having anyone notice he's eating too much fudge. That sounds small, but it isn't.

headlineQuote: I'm not putting the price of a loaf up because a man from the city has a new car.
portrait: Lena Silva is fifty-eight and runs Hartwell Farm, a mixed farm with cattle, sheep and vegetables, and a busy farm shop in the old cart shed with her partner Joao. She's a careful, warm progressive who protects her lowest-paid staff first and thinks in terms of the village. Halfway through the interview she realised the shop depends on office workers' wages, which made the office-job scenarios more worrying than she expected. She stays steady even with robots, waiting to see one work on a neighbour's farm before buying, and leaning harder into what people do best.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it would push down food prices at big farms while her customers lose their wages.
whatWouldHelp: The government sharing the gains so people still have money to spend locally, and help for small farms to buy robots together as a cooperative.
